a: Take your stand in the gateway of the LORD's house. Call out this word there. Say,
t: The gate of the LORD's house
p: The Greek has no setting for the sermon. A Qumran scroll agrees with the Hebrew.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); 4QJer-a (4Q70), which preserves "at the gate of the LORD's house and call out there"
readings.orig: עֲמֹד בְּשַׁעַר בֵּית יְהוָה וְקָרָאתָ שָׁם
readings.en: stand in the gate of the LORD's house and proclaim there
readings.plain: Take your stand in the gateway of the LORD's house. Call out this word there. Say,

readings.w: the Greek (Codex Vaticanus, as printed in Swete's edition)
readings.en: Hear the word of the LORD (no gate, no proclamation)

why: The Hebrew is the base text, and 4QJer-a, the scroll that mostly agrees with the Masoretic edition, has the gate. The Greek reflects the shorter edition of Jeremiah.
b: The Greek also lacks the opening line (7:1) and the end of 7:2, "you who pass through these gates to bow down to the LORD." Jeremiah 26:2 gives the setting in similar words.

a: "We are rescued!" You say it so you can go on doing all these abhorrent things.
t: "Rescued" or "kept away"?
p: The Greek has the worshipers say "We have kept away from all these abominations."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.orig: נִצַּלְנוּ לְמַעַן עֲשׂוֹת אֵת כָּל־הַתּוֹעֵבוֹת הָאֵלֶּה
readings.en: we are delivered, so as to do all these abominations
readings.plain: "We are rescued!" You say it so you can go on doing all these abhorrent things.

readings.w: the Greek (Codex Vaticanus, as printed in Swete's edition)
readings.orig: Ἀπεσχήμεθα τοῦ μὴ ποιεῖν πάντα τὰ βδελύγματα ταῦτα
readings.en: we have kept away from doing all these abominations
readings.plain: "We have kept away from doing all these abhorrent things."

why: The Plain follows the Hebrew. The Greek changes what the worshipers claim: not that they are safe, but that they are clean. The Hebrew is the harder reading, and its sharp "so as to" fits 7:4 and the charge in 7:9.
b: No scroll preserves 7:10. The Greek's wording is a different claim, not a different translation of the same words, so the note at "We are rescued!" (on the Hebrew lema'an) does not apply to it.

a: to make cakes for the Queen of Heaven
t: Queen of Heaven, or army of heaven?
p: The Greek says the cakes were for "the army of heaven."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: for the queen of the heavens
readings.plain: to make cakes for the Queen of Heaven

readings.w: the Greek (Codex Vaticanus, as printed in Swete's edition)
readings.en: for the army of heaven
readings.plain: to make kawwanim for the army of the heavens

why: The Hebrew Queen of Heaven is the harder reading and is repeated in 44:17–19, 25. The Greek may have changed it to the familiar worship of the stars (8:2; 19:13).
b: No scroll preserves this phrase. The Greek does not translate the Hebrew word for the cakes. It writes the word in Greek letters (chauonas), so the second reading shows the Hebrew word kawwanim.

a: I brought them out
t: "I brought them out" or "he brought them out"?
p: A written and a read form differ in person: "he brought" or "I brought."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008), read form (Qere); the Greek (Codex Vaticanus, as printed in Swete's edition), which has "I brought up" (anegagon)
readings.en: I brought out
readings.plain: I brought them out

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008), written form (Ketiv)
readings.en: he brought out
readings.plain: he brought them out

why: The read form fits the verse, where the LORD speaks in the first person ("I did not speak"), and the Greek agrees. The written form is probably a spelling without the final yod. 11:4 has the same word, hotsi'i.
b: No scroll preserves 7:22. In 11:4, 4QJer-a has the form with the final yod.

a: You will tell them all these words, but they will not listen to you. You will call out to them, but they will not answer you.
t: Verse 27 missing in the Greek
p: The Greek does not have this verse. No scroll preserves it.

readings.en: You will say to them all these words
readings.plain: You will tell them all these words, but they will not listen to you. You will call out to them, but they will not answer you.

readings.w: the Greek (Codex Vaticanus, as printed in Swete's edition)
readings.en: no verse

why: The verse is part of the long Hebrew edition, which the Plain follows. A reader of the Greek goes straight from 7:26 to 7:28.

a: they will bring out
t: "They will bring out" or "and they will bring out"?
p: A written form has an extra "and."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008), read form (Qere); 4QJer-a (4Q70), which has the word without the "and"; the Greek (Codex Vaticanus, as printed in Swete's edition)

readings.plain: they will bring out

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008), written form (Ketiv)
readings.en: and they will bring out
readings.plain: and they will bring out

why: The read form begins the clause cleanly after "At that time, the LORD declares," and a scroll and the Greek agree with it.

a: his own course
t: One course or many?
p: A written form is plural ("courses"), the read form singular.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008), read form (Qere); the Greek (Codex Vaticanus, as printed in Swete's edition), which has "his course"
readings.en: in their course
readings.plain: his own course

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008), written form (Ketiv)
readings.en: in their courses
readings.plain: their own courses

why: The singular matches "like a horse rushing into the fight." The difference is small.
b: 4QJer-a's word here is restored, so no scroll reading is cited.

a: the swift
t: Swift or horse?
p: A written form and a read form differ by one letter: "horse" or "swift."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008), read form (Qere)
readings.en: the swift (or swallow)
readings.plain: the swift

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008), written form (Ketiv); 4QJer-a (4Q70), which spells the word with a waw
readings.en: a horse
readings.plain: the horse

why: A bird fits the other three birds in the verse, and the Greek has a swallow (chelidon). The Ketiv's "horse" could be a scribe's slip for the bird.
b: The Masoretes wrote sus, "horse," and marked it to be read sis. The scroll's spelling agrees with the written form. That may be only a spelling of the same bird word, so the scroll does not settle it. The scroll also has "they keep" (yishmeru, with a prefix) where the Masoretic Text has shameru, a difference of tense that the English does not show.

a: every one grabs at gain he has no right to.
t: Verses 8:10b–12 in the Greek
p: The Greek does not have 8:10b–12, which repeat 6:12–15. A Qumran scroll has them. Entries for 8:10, 8:11 and 8:12 go together.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); 4QJer-a (4Q70)
readings.en: all of it is gaining unjust gain
readings.plain: every one grabs at gain he has no right to.

readings.w: the Greek (Codex Vaticanus, as printed in Swete's edition), which ends 8:10 after "to the heirs"
readings.en: no text

why: The Plain follows the Hebrew, supported by the scroll. The Greek has no 8:10b–12.
b: Because 4QJer-a, the scroll closest to the Masoretic Text, has these lines, the repetition of 6:12–15 is not a late Masoretic addition; but the Greek's source lacked them. Where the Hebrew is the same as 6:12–15, the Plain uses the same English; the note at 8:11 lists the real differences.

a: They have healed the broken place of my dear people
t: Verses 8:10b–12 in the Greek (continued)
p: This verse goes with 8:10 and 8:12. The Greek omits it; a scroll has it.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); 4QJer-a (4Q70)
readings.en: they have healed the fracture of the daughter of my people
readings.plain: They have healed the broken place of my dear people

readings.w: the Greek (Codex Vaticanus, as printed in Swete's edition)
readings.en: no text

p: This verse goes with 8:10 and 8:11. The Greek omits it; a scroll has it.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); 4QJer-a (4Q70)

readings.plain: Are they ashamed of the abhorrent thing they have done?

a: I will gather them up and sweep them away
t: Gathering them, or gathering their harvest?
p: The Greek reads "they will gather their produce." The scroll agrees with the Hebrew word for "gather them."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); 4QJer-a (4Q70), which preserves the second word, 'asifam
readings.en: gathering I will gather them (or: make an end of them)
readings.plain: I will gather them up and sweep them away

readings.w: the Greek (Codex Vaticanus, as printed in Swete's edition)
readings.en: and they will gather their produce
readings.plain: They will gather their produce

why: The Hebrew word is supported by the scroll's second word, and the Greek has read the same consonants as a harvest. The Hebrew is obscure, but the Greek rewrites the verse.
b: The first word of the Hebrew is restored in 4QJer-a, so it is not a scroll reading.

a: Their tongue is a hammered arrow.
t: A hammered or a deadly arrow?
p: A written and a read form differ: "hammered" or "slaughtering." This is Hebrew 9:7.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008), read form (Qere)
readings.en: a beaten (hammered) arrow
readings.plain: Their tongue is a hammered arrow.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008), written form (Ketiv)
readings.en: a slaughtering arrow
readings.plain: Their tongue is a deadly arrow.

why: The read form makes good sense: a hammered arrow is one beaten into shape, from the word used of hammered gold in 1 Kings 10:16. The Greek has "a wounding dart," closer to the Ketiv's idea.
b: 4QJer-a's word here is restored, so no scroll reading is cited.

a: Like a scarecrow in a cucumber field, they cannot speak.
t: A scarecrow, or worked silver?
p: The Greek has "it is worked silver" and lacks "they do not speak."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); 4QJer-b (4Q71), which preserves the whole verse
readings.en: like a scarecrow (or palm of turned work) in a cucumber field (or: of hammered work) they are, and they do not speak
readings.plain: Like a scarecrow in a cucumber field, they cannot speak.

readings.w: the Greek (Codex Vaticanus, as printed in Swete's edition)
readings.en: it is worked (hammered) silver
readings.plain: They are worked silver.

why: The Plain follows the Hebrew, and 4QJer-b agrees with it. The Greek seems to take miqshah as "hammered work" (the second reading in the note on this phrase) and goes its own way after it.
b: The Greek has no clause for "they do not speak."

a: You are great, and great is your name in strength.
t: Verses 10:6–8 and 10:10 in the short edition
p: The Greek and one Qumran scroll lack 10:6–8 and 10:10. Entries for 10:6, 10:7, 10:8 and 10:10 go together.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008). No scroll preserves 10:6–8
readings.en: you are great, and your name is great in might
readings.plain: You are great, and great is your name in strength.

readings.w: the Greek (Codex Vaticanus, as printed in Swete's edition); 4QJer-b (4Q71), which has 10:1–5 and 10:9 but not 10:6–8 or 10:10
readings.en: no verses

why: The Plain follows the Hebrew Masoretic edition. The omission is shared by the Greek and by 4QJer-b, two independent witnesses to a shorter edition; 4QJer-a (4Q70) has 10:10 like the Masoretic Text. The witnesses are split, which is the best evidence that two editions of Jeremiah circulated at Qumran.
b: Both lines of 10:6 are lost in the short edition. The entry shows only the second line, because that is the line the anchor covers; the first line ("There is no one like you, LORD") goes with it. Tov takes the shorter text as the earlier edition. 4QJer-b is a Qumran copy of the second century BC (published estimates run from about 200 BC to the middle of the century), and the transcription preserves it from 9:23 to 10:21.

a: Who would not be afraid of you, king of the nations?
t: Verses 10:6–8 and 10:10 in the short edition (continued)
p: This verse goes with 10:6. The Greek and 4QJer-b omit it.

t: A shorter line and a different order
p: The Greek and 4QJer-b lack "the work of a craftsman" and put "the work of the wise" before the colors.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); 4QJer-a (4Q70), which has the order of the Masoretic Text
readings.en: the work of a craftsman and the hands of a metalsmith
readings.plain: the work of a craftsman and of a metalsmith's hands.

readings.w: 4QJer-b (4Q71), as transcribed; the Greek (Codex Vaticanus, as printed in Swete's edition)
readings.en: the hands of a metalsmith
readings.plain: the hands of a metalsmith.

why: The Plain follows the Masoretic Text. The scroll and the Greek share a shorter text, which fits their shared short text of 10:6–8 and 10:10.
b: In 4QJer-b, as Abegg, Bowley and Cook transcribe it, "the work of the wise, all of them" comes before the colored cloth, and the Greek has the same order ("works of craftsmen, all of them; they put violet and purple on them"). In the Masoretic Text and 4QJer-a that phrase comes last.

a: But the LORD is God in truth.
t: Verses 10:6–8 and 10:10 in the short edition (continued)
p: The Greek and 4QJer-b omit this verse. 4QJer-a has it.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); 4QJer-a (4Q70)

readings.plain: But the LORD is God in truth.

readings.en: no verse

why: See 10:6. 4QJer-a preserves the end of the verse as the Masoretic Text has it, though some words are restored.

a: and he leads the wind out of its storerooms
t: Wind or light?
p: The Hebrew says wind. The Greek says light. A scroll agrees with the Hebrew.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); 4QJer-b (4Q71), which has the word
readings.en: and he brings out wind from his storehouses
readings.plain: and he leads the wind out of its storerooms

readings.w: the Greek (Codex Vaticanus, as printed in Swete's edition)
readings.orig: καὶ ἐξήγαγεν φῶς ἐκ θησαυρῶν αὐτοῦ
readings.en: and he brought out light from his storehouses
readings.plain: and he leads light out of its storerooms

why: Psalm 135:7 and Jeremiah 51:16 read "wind" in the same line, and 4QJer-b has the Hebrew word whole.
b: In the same verse the written form (Ketiv) has "earth" without the article (erets, not ha-arets) in "the end of the earth," and the read form (Qere) has the article. 4QJer-a, 4QJer-b and 4QJer-c all have the form without the article, as the written form does; the English is the same either way.

a: Pick your bundle up off the ground,
t: A different verse in the Greek
p: The Greek reads this verse very differently. The scroll agrees with the Hebrew.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); 4QJer-b (4Q71)
readings.en: gather up from the ground your bundle
readings.plain: Pick your bundle up off the ground,

readings.w: the Greek (Codex Vaticanus, as printed in Swete's edition)
readings.en: he has gathered your property from outside
readings.plain: He has gathered your goods from outside,

why: The Hebrew has an imperative addressed to a woman (Zion). The Greek has a statement about someone gathering her goods, and its next words ("dwelling among the chosen") differ in the same way. The scroll supports the Hebrew.
b: The Greek's next words also differ: "dwelling among the chosen" where the Hebrew has "you who sit under siege." In the Hebrew, the written form (Ketiv) of "you who sit" is an old feminine form (yoshavti); the read form (Qere) is yoshevet. 4QJer-b spells the read form (with a waw).

a: I gave your ancestors a strong warning on the day I brought them up out of the land of Egypt, and I have kept on warning them to this day, rising early to do it. I said, Listen to my voice.

a: Can holy meat make your evil pass away from you,
t: Vows and holy meat
p: The Hebrew has "the many" in the line before. The Greek has "vows" with the holy meat.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: and holy flesh will pass away from you
readings.plain: Can holy meat make your evil pass away from you,

readings.w: the Greek (Codex Vaticanus, as printed in Swete's edition)
readings.orig: μὴ εὐχαὶ καὶ κρέα ἅγια ἀφελοῦσιν
readings.en: will vows and holy meat take your evils away from you
readings.plain: Can vows and holy meat make your evil pass away from you,

why: The Hebrew is hard and the Greek reads more smoothly, which could mean the Greek is a repair or that the Hebrew has a scribal slip ("the many," harabbim, for "the vows," hannedarim). No scroll preserves the verse. The Plain follows the Hebrew and shows the Greek.
b: The next entry belongs with this one. The Greek then ends the verse with "or by these will you escape?", which the Hebrew does not have.

p: The Greek has "What has the beloved done in my house? An abomination!" This goes with the entry below it.

readings.w: the Greek (Codex Vaticanus, as printed in Swete's edition)
readings.en: she has done an abomination
readings.plain: when she has done an abomination?

why: See the entry above. No scroll preserves the verse.

a: a tame lamb
t: Tame lamb or innocent lamb?
p: The Greek has "an innocent lamb." Rashi reports other readings of the Hebrew word.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008). No scroll preserves these words
readings.en: like a tame (or large, or leader-) lamb
readings.plain: a tame lamb

readings.w: the Greek (Codex Vaticanus, as printed in Swete's edition)
readings.en: like an innocent (harmless) lamb
readings.plain: an innocent lamb

why: The Plain follows the Hebrew. The Greek reads aluf as "gentle" or "innocent," as the BSB, ASV and WEB also render it. Rashi reports other readings: Menahem took it as "large lamb," Targum Jonathan has "choice lamb," and Dunash and Judah ben Kudish read "lamb and ox."

a: Let us ruin the tree along with its bread.
t: Ruin the tree, or put wood in his bread?
p: The Greek has "put wood into his bread"; 4QJer-a has the Masoretic verb.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); 4QJer-a (4Q70), which preserves these words unbroken

readings.plain: Let us ruin the tree along with its bread.

readings.w: the Greek (Codex Vaticanus, as printed in Swete's edition)
readings.orig: ἐμβάλωμεν ξύλον εἰς τὸν ἄρτον αὐτοῦ
readings.en: let us put wood into his bread
readings.plain: Let us put wood into his bread.

why: The Plain follows the Hebrew, and a Qumran copy has the same words. The Greek verb means "put in," not "destroy," so the Greek translator read a different verb or paraphrased. "Tree" and "bread" are the same in both.
b: This Greek wording is the one the early Christian writers quote (see the note on this verse). Rashi, who read the Hebrew, understands "wood in his bread" as poison put in his food.

a: He will not see our end.

p: The Greek says "God will not see our ways." A scroll has "our end" with an odd verb form.

readings.en: he will not see our end
readings.plain: He will not see our end.

readings.w: the Greek (Codex Vaticanus, as printed in Swete's edition)
readings.en: God will not see our ways
readings.plain: God will not see our ways.

why: The noun "our end" is the Hebrew reading in the MT and in the scroll. The Greek "ways" could be a different reading or a repair, and it names the subject.
b: Whom the Hebrew "he" means is discussed in the note.

a: feel secure
t: Secure, stumbling, or not trusting?
p: The Greek says "you have not trusted." Some English versions read "stumble."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); 4QJer-a (4Q70), which preserves the same consonants unbroken
readings.en: trusting, secure
readings.plain: feel secure

readings.w: The same Hebrew letters read as "fall, stumble", as in the BSB and the NIV; the project's word-by-word line also glosses the word "falling"
readings.en: stumbling, falling
readings.plain: stumble

readings.w: the Greek (Codex Vaticanus, as printed in Swete's edition)
readings.en: you have not trusted
readings.plain: have not felt secure

why: The Plain keeps the ordinary meaning of the Hebrew word, "trust, feel secure," which the KJV, ASV, WEB and YLT also give. The consonants are certain (4QJer-a has them). The Greek adds a negative, which reverses the logic of the verse.
b: The second reading is a different understanding of the same consonants, not a different manuscript. It makes the argument sharper: if even a safe land trips you, what of the thicket by the Jordan. The Greek is Codex Vaticanus in Swete's edition; a critical edition such as Ziegler's was not checked for this word.

a: Is my inheritance a speckled bird of prey to me?
t: Bird of prey or hyena?
p: The Hebrew has a speckled bird of prey. The Greek has a hyena's cave.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: is my inheritance to me a speckled bird of prey?
readings.plain: Is my inheritance a speckled bird of prey to me?

readings.w: the Greek (Codex Vaticanus, as printed in Swete's edition)
readings.orig: μὴ σπήλαιον ὑαίνης ἡ κληρονομία μου ἐμοί
readings.en: is my inheritance to me a hyena's cave?
readings.plain: Is my inheritance a hyena's cave to me?

why: The Hebrew word is rare, and the next line ("birds of prey circling") fits the bird reading. No scroll preserves the verse.
b: The Greek has "cave" in both clauses ("a hyena's cave" and "a cave round about her"), so the second clause, where the Hebrew has birds of prey circling, is also a difference. The Plain follows the Hebrew in both.
